title: The Prime 2: Order of 1 + 2·a and the Non-Cyclicity of (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ

meta.author: classical number theory; formalized for lean-genius

mathlibDependencies.description: For odd a, orderOf (1 + 4·a : ZMod (2^(n+2))) = 2^n — the p=2 analogue of the parent's order formula, with 4·a (not 2·a)
orderOf (5 : ZMod (2^(n+2))) = 2^n — the principal-unit generator of order 2^(k-2)
(ZMod (2^k))ˣ is cyclic iff k ≤ 2; re-exported as the cyclicity dichotomy. The file gives an independent two-involution proof of the k ≥ 3 (non-cyclic) direction.
In a finite cyclic group, the number of elements of order d equals φ(d); with d = 2 this gives a unique involution, the engine of the non-cyclicity proof
orderOf (-1) = if ringChar R = 2 then 1 else 2; gives orderOf(-1) = 2 since ringChar (ZMod 2^k) = 2^k ≠ 2
x^p = 1 and x ≠ 1 imply orderOf x = p; used to show the special involution 1 + 2^(k-1) has order 2

originalContributions: not_isCyclic_units_two_pow: an explicit, constructive proof that (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ is not cyclic for k ≥ 3, by exhibiting two distinct elements of order 2 (−1 and 1 + 2^(k-1)) and invoking that a cyclic group has exactly φ(2) = 1 involution. This is a different, more elementary proof architecture than Mathlib's isCyclic_units_two_pow_iff (which reduces through a surjection onto (ℤ/8ℤ)ˣ).

orderOf_one_add_two_pow: the special involution 1 + 2^(k-1) has multiplicative order exactly 2 modulo 2^k (its square is 1 + 2^k + 2^(2k-2) ≡ 1), proved via a natural-number ModEq congruence, axiom-free.
neg_one_ne_one_add_two_pow: the two canonical involutions −1 and 1 + 2^(k-1) are distinct precisely for k ≥ 3 (they coincide only at k = 2), pinned down by the residue bound 0 < 2 + 2^(k-1) < 2^k.

Honest framing of the open question: for p = 2 the clean order formula is carried by 1 + 4·a (a odd), not 1 + 2·a — the residue of 1 + 2·a mod 4 already splits the units into two cosets, only one of which (≡ 1 mod 4) attains the maximal 2-power order 2^(k-2). This is the precise sense in which '1 + 2·a behaves differently' from the odd-prime case.
Concrete instances orderOf(-1 : ZMod 8) = 2, orderOf(5 : ZMod 8) = 2, and ¬ IsCyclic (ZMod 8)ˣ, all derived from the general theorems (no native_decide).
meta.assumptions: None. Fully verified, 0 axioms, 0 sorries; depends only on the standard foundational axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The order formulas for 1 + 4·a and the cyclicity dichotomy are re-exported from Mathlib's ZMod.UnitsCyclic; the non-cyclicity result is reproved here by the explicit two-involution argument rather than re-exported.

conclusion.summary: At the prime 2 the structure of (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ departs from the odd-prime case in two linked ways. First, the maximal 2-power order is no longer carried by every 1 + 2·a: the clean order formula orderOf(1 + 4·a) = 2^(k-2) (a odd) needs the 1 + 4·a form, because the residue of 1 + 2·a modulo 4 already splits the units into the squares (≡ 1 mod 4) and the −1 coset (≡ 3 mod 4). Second, and as a consequence, the unit group is not cyclic for k ≥ 3: it carries two distinct involutions, −1 and 1 + 2^(k-1), whereas a cyclic group has exactly one. The file proves the non-cyclicity by exhibiting these two order-2 elements and counting involutions via φ(2) = 1.
implications: Isolates the prime 2 (powers ≥ 3) as the unique prime-power modulus whose unit group fails to be cyclic, complementing the parent's odd-prime order computation.
Gives a fully constructive obstruction to cyclicity — a named pair of involutions — rather than an abstract reduction, making the failure of cyclicity transparent.
Locates the maximal cyclic subgroup ⟨5⟩ of order 2^(k-2) inside (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ, the 2-adic analogue of the principal units 1 + pℤ for odd p.
openQuestions: Can one package the full isomorphism (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ ≃ ℤ/2 × ℤ/2^(k-2) for k ≥ 3, with explicit generators −1 and 5, mirroring the odd-prime isomorphism (ℤ/pᵏℤ)ˣ ≃ ℤ/p^(k-1) × ℤ/(p-1)?
What is the exact multiplicative order of a general 1 + 2·a modulo 2^k as a function of the 2-adic valuation v₂(a) and v₂(a+1), uniformly covering both the ⟨5⟩ coset and the −1 coset?
